title: The Disappearers
author: Marlon James
review: Three generations, one vanishing act. James writes violence and tenderness in the same breath — nothing else this year comes close.

title: The New Dark Ages
author: James Marriott
review: A bracing, argumentative case that we have stopped reading. You will disagree with half of it and finish it in a sitting.

title: Redwood
author: Ben Macintyre
review: Macintyre at his best: a spy story that turns on one man's nerve, told with the pace of a thriller and the footnotes of a historian.

title: The Strangers
author: Naomi Alderman
review: Something is wrong in the allotments. Alderman builds dread out of compost heaps and shed doors — deeply English, deeply unsettling.

title: Exit Party
author: Emily St. John Mandel
review: Mandel again finds the quiet centre of a loud catastrophe. Pitched somewhere between elegy and heist.

title: Taipei Story
author: Rebecca F. Kuang
review: Kuang turns her eye on inheritance and the objects we leave behind. Precise, cool, and quietly devastating.

title: No Land to Stand On
author: Mahmoud Khalil
review: Written from the inside of a situation most of us only read about. Urgent, careful, and impossible to put aside.

title: How to be Hopeful
author: Caitlin Moran
review: Funny in the way that only someone taking it seriously can be. Moran on the mechanics of not giving up.

title: Prisoners of Geography
author: Tim Marshall
review: Ten maps, ten arguments about why nations behave as they do. The book that makes the news make sense.

title: Black and British
author: David Olusoga
review: The history you were not taught, told with Olusoga's particular gift for making the archive feel like the present tense.

title: The Shock Doctrine
author: Naomi Klein
review: Twenty years on and still the sharpest account of how crises get used. A book that rearranges how you read a headline.

title: Fight Oligarchy
author: Bernie Sanders
review: Blunt, unhedged, and refreshingly free of the usual hand-wringing. Sanders makes his case and gets out.

title: Farewell to Eden
author: Sebastian Faulks
review: Faulks on the small betrayals that decide a life. The Levant setting is beautifully done and never merely scenic.

title: Stories
author: Annie Proulx
review: Four decades of Proulx in one volume. Landscape as character, sentences you re-read for the pleasure of the construction.

title: Big Swiss
author: Jen Beagin
review: Improbably funny about grief, sex and eavesdropping. Beagin's narrator is the best company in fiction right now.

title: Cloud Atlas
author: David Mitchell
review: Six nested lives, six voices, one argument about cruelty and repetition. Still the most ambitious novel on this shelf.

title: The Bell Jar
author: Sylvia Plath
review: As clear-eyed and modern as the day it was published. Plath on ambition, illness and the cost of being watched.

title: Beloved
author: Toni Morrison
review: Morrison at full power. A ghost story about what slavery did to love — the finest American novel of its century.

title: Not Too Late
author: Rebecca Solnit
review: An antidote to climate despair that never once talks down to you. Solnit gathers the people already doing the work.

title: Wild Fell
author: Lee Schofield
review: One farm, one decade, one honest account of what rewilding actually costs. Schofield is very good on failure.

title: The Salt Path
author: Raynor Winn
review: Homeless and walking the coast path. It should be bleak; it is the most life-affirming thing we have sold in years.

title: H is for Hawk
author: Helen Macdonald
review: Grief, falconry and T. H. White. Macdonald's prose has the same tautness as the jesses on her wrist.

title: Underland
author: Robert Macfarlane
review: Macfarlane goes down instead of up. Catacombs, glaciers, fungal networks — the book that changed how we talk about landscape.

title: Wilding
author: Isabella Tree
review: What happened when they let a Sussex estate go. Tree makes ecological recovery read like a thriller with turtle doves in it.
